# How to Alert or Open a Ticket When an Expected Client File Does Not Arrive

 Donal Tobin 

 12 min read Jun 18, 2026 

Table of Contents

- The Problem with Manual File Monitoring
- What You Will Need Before Starting
- How to Alert When an Expected Client File Does Not Arrive: Step-by-Step
- Common Mistakes to Avoid
- Conclusion

You alert or open a ticket when an expected client file does not arrive by building a file-arrival check that runs on a schedule, compares what was expected against what actually landed, and triggers a notification or creates a support ticket automatically when the file is missing or late. This guide is for data engineers and operations teams who depend on clients delivering files on a predictable schedule and need to catch late or missing deliveries before they cause downstream failures. By the end, you will have a monitoring pipeline that detects missing file delivery, fires an alert to your team, and optionally opens a ticket in your support or project management system without any manual checking.

Without this system, a missing file often goes unnoticed until someone asks why a report is stale or a downstream job failed with a zero-row source.

# We read the partner's file while they were still writing it 

At 14:07 on a Tuesday, four thousand three hundred products went out of stock on our storefront. Nothing had happened in the warehouse. Our hourly inventory import had read a file that was still being uploaded.

Our logistics partner drops a full inventory snapshot into an SFTP directory every hour, about seven megabytes, written straight to its final name. Our poller lists the directory every sixty seconds, takes anything matching the pattern, imports it, deletes it. For two years the upload finished in under ten seconds and the race never came up. That afternoon their link was slow, the write took over a minute, and our poller walked in halfway through.

The import did not fail. It read a perfectly valid CSV that happened to stop after sixty-one percent of the rows, and because the file is a snapshot rather than a set of changes, every product missing from it was treated as having no stock. We applied it in a single transaction exactly as designed. It was correct according to the only rule anyone had given it.

## How Files.com Fits With Celigo

An iPaaS earns its keep on record-level work: read the file, map the fields, create the NetSuite transaction. The file side of the same integration is a different job. Counterparties arrive with protocol mandates, PGP keys get pasted connection by connection, and an SFTP server somebody has to run sits under it all for the flows to poll. Building that side out of flow steps hardcodes every partner quirk into the integration.

# 🚨 P1 Production Incident | 18 GB SFTP File Transfer Running Extremely Slow · 2026-08-18T00:00:00+00:00

🚨 P1 Production Incident | 18 GB SFTP File Transfer Running Extremely Slow
Imagine receiving a P1 ticket at 2:00 AM:
“Critical 18 GB settlement file is transferring very slowly. Business SLA is at risk.”
The first question from many teams is:
❓ “Is the network bandwidth okay?”
The network team confirms:
✅ 1 Gbps bandwidth available
✅ Network is UP
✅ No major packet loss
✅ Sterling nodes are healthy
But the file is still transferring at only ~150 Mbps.
So, where is the bottleneck?
🔍 My P1 troubleshooting approach
1️⃣ Check the Business Process
Is the BP running continuously, or is it waiting?
Look for:
WAITING_ON_IO
SFTP PUT/GET delays
Retries
Long gaps between BP steps
2️⃣ Check the SFTP session
Is the remote server accepting data normally?
Check:
Session status
Transfer activity
Remote filesystem
Connection limits
Partner-side performance
3️⃣ Check Network Performance
Don't stop at “network is UP.”
Look at:
RTT / latency
TCP window scaling
Packet retransmissions
Throughput
Cross-region latency
4️⃣ Check CPU & Encryption
SFTP uses SSH encryption.
For a large file, encryption overhead can become significant if the system is already under CPU pressure.
5️⃣ Check Disk I/O
The network may support 1 Gbps, but if storage is writing much slower, the transfer will still be slow.
Check:
Read/write latency
IOPS
Disk utilization
Filesystem performance

# We were the unreliable half of the integration 

On a Tuesday our carrier partner suspended our event subscription. Around fourteen thousand shipment updates over nine hours were never sent to us, and we learned about it from a customer asking why their tracking page had not moved since breakfast.

Their delivery platform grades the systems it delivers to. The rule is written in their documentation, in a section I had read four years ago as a paragraph about them: a receiver that takes longer than five seconds to answer is recorded as a failed delivery, and a subscription with more than a hundred consecutive failures is suspended until its owner switches it back on in their portal. All of that is sensible, and none of us had ever considered that our end of an integration carried a service level, measured by another company, against a number nobody here had looked up.

Our handler did everything inside the request. Check the event, load the shipment, update three rows, write an audit record. Two hundred milliseconds on an ordinary morning.
